topicName: Basic Networking Concepts (IP Addressing, Subnetting, DNS)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Basic Networking Concepts in Linux System Administration"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding networking is crucial for any Linux system administrator. This tutorial covers fundamental concepts: IP addressing, subnetting, and DNS."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"IP Addressing"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An IP (Internet Protocol) address is a numerical label assigned to each device participating in a computer network that uses the Internet Protocol for communication. It acts as a unique identifier for a device on a network."},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"There are two main versions of IP addresses: IPv4 and IPv6. IPv4 addresses are 32-bit numerical addresses, typically written in dotted decimal notation (e.g., 192.168.1.1). IPv6 addresses are 128-bit alphanumeric addresses, written in hexadecimal notation (e.g., 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334)."},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"IP addresses can be either static or dynamic. Static IP addresses are manually assigned and remain constant. Dynamic IP addresses are assigned automatically by a DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) server and can change over time."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"# Display IP address information using 'ip addr' command:
ip addr"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Subnetting"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Subnetting is the practice of dividing a network into two or more smaller networks. This is done to improve network performance, security, and manageability."},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"A subnet mask is used to identify the network and host portions of an IP address. It's a 32-bit number that, when 'ANDed' with an IP address, reveals the network address. For example, a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0 indicates that the first three octets of the IP address represent the network address, and the last octet represents the host address."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) notation is a shorthand way to represent subnet masks. It specifies the number of bits in the network portion of the IP address. For example, /24 is equivalent to a subnet mask of 255.255.255.0."},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Example: If an IP address is 192.168.1.10/24, the network address is 192.168.1.0, and the host address is 10."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"DNS (Domain Name System)"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"DNS is a hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or any resource connected to the Internet or a private network. It translates human-readable domain names (e.g., google.com) into IP addresses (e.g., 142.250.185.142) that computers use to communicate."},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"DNS servers are organized in a hierarchical structure, with root servers at the top, followed by top-level domain (TLD) servers (e.g., .com, .org, .net), and then authoritative name servers for specific domains."},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"When you type a domain name into your web browser, your computer queries a DNS server to resolve the domain name to an IP address. This process is called DNS resolution."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# Use 'nslookup' or 'dig' to query DNS servers:
nslookup google.com
dig google.com"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"nslookup: A tool for querying DNS servers to obtain domain name or IP address mapping information."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"dig: A more advanced DNS lookup utility that provides more detailed information than nslookup."},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"The /etc/resolv.conf file on Linux systems specifies the DNS servers that the system should use for name resolution."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"# Example /etc/resolv.conf:
nameserver 8.8.8.8
nameserver 8.8.4.4"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, the system is configured to use Google's public DNS servers (8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4)."},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"These basic networking concepts are fundamental for managing and troubleshooting Linux systems. A solid understanding of IP addressing, subnetting, and DNS is essential for any Linux system administrator."}]
